children: The sounds of the train that makes frequent interruptions during Molly’s monologue in “Penelope” is a crucial component to the chapter. Since Molly’s stream of consciousness takes place in a long-winded format lacking in punctuality or grammar, our sense of time and pacing as reader’s can go askew. The onomatopoeia of the train reconnects Molly with the physical background that she exists in outside of her mind. In another interpretation, the train can be viewed as a patriarchal element, one which constantly interrupts Molly AKA the only female narrator in Ulysses. However, Molly’s persistence of thought despite the train’s ruckus displays her steadfast nature.

According to Don Gifford, the Cameron Highlanders were stationed in Gibraltar and the statue was in Alameda Gardens in Gibraltar.  So, Molly has flashed back to growing up in Gibraltar.
The Highlanders were relieved by the Surreys in 1882. So, Molly must have been under the age of twelve when the men exposed themselves to her.
Also, Gifford says that the statue was removed from the park in 1884, so Molly must have been very young when this happened.

children: “Taittering of the lips,” apparently, was Irish vernacular for quivering of the vulva. Joyce seems to have found the expression in Havelock Ellis,
Studies in the Psychology of Sex

Even in the absence of sexual excitement there is a vague affection, occurring in both married and unmarried women, and not, it would seem, necessarily hysterical, characterized by quivering or twitching of the vulva; I am told that this is popularly termed “flackering of the shape” in Yorkshire and “taittering of the lips” in Ireland.
It’s unclear whether Molly invokes this meaning on purpose or if Joyce is having his own fun at Molly’s expense.
